common_name: Cashmere Bouquet (Chinese Glory Bower, Double Clerodendrum)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock after frost danger has passed in fertile, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in part sun; give this vigorous shrub room to spread since it suckers freely from underground roots and can naturalize a bed within a couple of seasons.

directions: Cashmere Bouquet is a suckering, colony-forming shrub grown for its dense, rounded terminal clusters of fully double, pom-pom-like flowers that open pale pink from deeper rose-pink buds and carry a sweet, carnation-like fragrance carried well beyond the plant on warm evenings. The large, softly felted, dark-green leaves have a rougher, more textured surface than the smooth foliage of Clerodendrum bungei, and because the double flowers are sterile the plant spreads only by root suckers rather than seed, so it stays where it is planted without becoming a seeding nuisance. Bloom is heaviest from late summer into fall. In marginal zone 9 sites the top growth is often killed by frost but the roots reliably resprout from the base once soil warms in spring.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in bright, filtered shade in organic-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil; protect from direct midday sun, which scorches the narrow leaves, and from cold, since this species is more tropical and less cold-hardy than most other cultivated Clerodendrum.

directions: Bridal Veil is grown for its long, narrow, pointed leaves and graceful, cascading racemes of small, fragrant, pure-white flowers that dangle from the branch tips like strings of tiny bells rather than forming the upright or balloon-like clusters typical of Clerodendrum thomsoniae or C. paniculatum. Unusually for a tropical shrub, it blooms heaviest from late fall into winter, giving color in the garden or as a hanging container specimen when few other Clerodendrum are flowering. It prefers steady moisture and bright shade year-round and resents both hot direct sun and cold, wet soil, making it better suited to a protected patio or greenhouse north of the warmest coastal zones.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container stock or rooted cuttings in average, well-drained soil in full to part sun after frost; site it at the back of a border where its tall, mostly unbranched canes can rise above shorter companions, and be ready to thin the colony since it spreads by rhizomes.

directions: Turk's Turban sends up tall, slender, nearly unbranched canes ringed in whorls of narrow leaves, each cane topped in late summer and fall by an airy spray of long, tubular, pure-white flowers with slender protruding stamens that radiate outward like a firework burst. As each flower fades, the star-shaped calyx behind it enlarges and flushes deep red, cradling a shining blue-black berry, so a single stem can show white blooms, red calyces, and dark berries simultaneously for a striking multi-stage display. It spreads by underground rhizomes to form an upright colony rather than a rounded shrub, and works best massed at the back of a bed or along a fence line where its height and airy texture read well from a distance.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; give this variegated form a bit more light than the solid-green species to keep the leaf pattern crisp, but still avoid harsh midday sun, which can scorch the pale leaf sections.

directions: This sport of the standard bleeding heart vine carries the same pendant clusters of white-calyx, red-corolla flowers as the species, but its real year-round appeal is foliage marbled in irregular patches of cream, chartreuse, and deep green, so the vine reads as a bright accent on a shaded trellis or porch even between bloom cycles. Growth is noticeably slower and less rampant than the plain green form, making it a more manageable choice for a container or a small arbor. Like its parent it twines rather than climbing by tendrils, so it needs to be tied in or woven onto its support, and it flowers most heavily in spring and again in fall.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
University of Hawaii College of Tropical Agriculture

common_name: Compact Peregrina (Dwarf Jatropha, Dwarf Spicy Jatropha)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light part shade; the naturally dwarf, dense habit needs little to no pruning to stay compact, making it a low-maintenance choice for foundation plantings, borders, and large containers where the full-size species would quickly outgrow the space.

directions: Compact Peregrina is a naturally dwarf selection of Jatropha integerrima that produces the same dense clusters of bright scarlet, star-shaped flowers over dark-green foliage almost continuously in warm weather, but on a tight, rounded frame that tops out around 4 to 6 feet rather than the 8 to 10 feet of the standard species. Because it holds its compact shape without regular shearing, it is far better suited than the full-size peregrina to small landscapes, mixed borders, and container culture on a patio. CAUTION: as with all Jatropha, the sap and seeds are toxic if ingested, so site it away from areas where children or pets forage.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or plant container-grown specimens in moist, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun after frost; grow it alongside the red-flowered species and white firespike for a layered fall hummingbird display in a shaded Gulf Coast bed.

directions: Pink Firespike shares the upright habit, glossy dark-green leaves, and long, tubular fall flower spikes of standard red firespike, but its blooms open in a soft rosy-pink rather than scarlet, giving gardeners a gentler color option for shaded beds that still delivers the same heavy fall nectar flow for migrating hummingbirds. It performs identically to the red form in cultivation, dying back to the roots in zone 9 winters and returning reliably each spring, and combines well with both the red species and Odontonema callistachyum for a multi-color firespike planting.
sources: Friends of Mercer Arboretum & Botanic Gardens
